A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DSG research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original visual question-answering experiments, component ablations, model comparisons and free-response evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix A.

after.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations and ablations, including additional reasoning controls, schema-complexity experiments and a human schema-quality study.

M1.justification: The three-stage DSG procedure, hierarchical grounding and final use of grounding history remain unchanged. Appendix C retains the same schema-generation prompt and twelve schemas. GPT-4o is a different evaluated backbone; the additional experimental variants do not revise the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: VAD is renamed VAB but retains 180 images, 540 questions, twelve concepts, four categories and both response formats. Appendix C.3 adds a distinct human task assessing schema representativeness and completeness, without expanding the visual benchmark's domains.

E2.justification: GPT-4o replaces GPT-4V in the principal comparisons, while GPT-4V's overall results survive in Section 5. Tables 9–10 add component-only single-round CoT, question-only and language-with-grounded-schema comparators. The full-schema single-round comparator matches the existing '+ schema' ablation rather than constituting another new baseline.

E3.justification: The primary evaluations and ablations switch from GPT-4V to GPT-4o. Appendix A.2 adds GPT-4-based correctness judging alongside BERTScore. New protocols control image access, vary example-schema size across 3, 5, 7 and 9 components, and collect three judgments on twelve schemas from twenty participants, yielding 720 responses.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and qualitative examples, Appendices A.3–A.5 examine single-round alternatives, the contribution of visual input and grounded context, and sensitivity to schema complexity. Appendix C.3 directly evaluates perceived schema quality with humans. These substantially broaden the checks on DSG's design and assumptions.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five-run averaging and report standard deviations for category comparisons in Tables 2 and 5. Added repeated model comparisons follow the same five-run practice. No new seed-reporting practice, confidence interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes from GPT-4V/DSG accuracies of 0.653/0.707 to GPT-4o/DSG accuracies of 0.664/0.730; these use different backbones. Tables 2, 3, 6 and 7 also replace results. In v2 Table 3, sequential grounding scores 0.727 on counting versus full DSG's 0.704, whereas full DSG led counting in v1. Tables 8–13 add evaluator, control, complexity and human-study results; v1's category-level free-response BERTScores are removed.

T1.justification: The VQA formulation, DAG-based schema definition and graded-accuracy formula are retained. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the added experiments and prompt examples introduce no new mathematical theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: DSG improves visual abstraction reasoning through explicit hierarchical schemas, is model-agnostic, and accompanies a visual abstraction benchmark. Updated headline scores provide different empirical support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: The main discussion retains its spatial-grounding, bias and schema-ambiguity limitations. New appendix interpretations discuss potentially misleading components in binary questions, dependence on example-prompt complexity, difficulties grounding detailed schemas, and benefits of explicit multi-round execution. The human study adds a qualified interpretation of schema alignment with human expectations.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents image-search sources, selection criteria and question construction. Appendix A.5 supplies expanded example prompts, and C.3 provides survey questions and participant counts. These improve documentation; the original schema prompt, inference-only setup, A40 hardware disclosure and dataset-access link remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds Kamalloo et al. (2023), Wei et al. (2022) and OpenAI's GPT-4o reference to support the new evaluator and comparisons. Section 2's substantive research positioning remains stable; several other reference changes merely update publication metadata or formatting.

P1.justification: V2 consistently renames Dataset/VAD to Benchmark/VAB, refines introductory explanations and grammar, and provides more specific appendix references. New subsections extend the existing appendix structure, while the main narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The appendix substantially expands its evidence displays with tables for GPT-4 judging, reasoning rounds, language controls, schema complexity, generated schema lengths and human ratings (Tables 8–13), while removing the earlier category-level free-response table. Figure 1 redraws grounded schemas as component mappings. Other figures are retained, with appendix figures and schema listings relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important validation gaps in v1: language controls test dependence on visual evidence, complexity experiments test a previously fixed design choice, and the human study directly assesses perceived schema quality. These additions substantially strengthen the empirical justification and expose limitations, independently of the higher GPT-4o scores. Removing the category-level free-response breakdown reduces detail, but the new controls and validation provide a clear overall gain.
